opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a hard decision, because both places were fantastic and I had a lot of respect for the people at CMU. In the end, it came down to people and fit more than rankings.

When I visited UW, I really clicked with the faculty I'd be working with. I had been doing machine learning research, things like the early work that became XGBoost, and I wanted to keep pushing on ML while also getting closer to systems. UW felt like a place where those two worlds were starting to come together. There was this sense that you could build real things, not just write papers, and that the boundaries between ML, systems, and even hardware weren't rigid.

The environment mattered too. Seattle had a growing tech ecosystem, and the department felt collaborative, a bit younger in spirit, very open to students trying unconventional directions. I remember thinking that if I wanted to do something that didn't fit neatly into one box, UW would let me.

Looking back, that turned out to matter a lot. A lot of what I ended up working on, like TVM and the machine learning compilation stack, was exactly that kind of cross-cutting work between ML and systems. I'm not sure it would have happened the same way somewhere else. So I'd say I picked the place where I felt I could grow in the direction I cared about, and I'm really glad I did.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and honestly, at the time it wasn't an obvious decision. CMU has an incredible machine learning program, and I was very tempted.

But a few things tipped it toward UW for me. The first was the advisors. I had the chance to work with Carlos Guestrin, and the environment in his group was very much about building real systems that people actually use, not just publishing papers. That resonated with me because even back then, during my undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong, I was already spending a lot of time building things like XGBoost, and I wanted a place where that kind of work was valued rather than seen as a distraction from "real research."

The second thing was the systems culture at UW. The computer science department there had a very strong systems group, and the boundary between machine learning and systems was quite porous. People like Luis Ceze were right there, and I ended up co-advised by him. That intersection, machine learning on one side and compilers and hardware on the other, is exactly where projects like MXNet and later TVM came from. I don't think I could have planned that out in advance, but I had a feeling that being in a department where I could just walk down the hall and talk to systems people would open up directions I couldn't predict.

And then, to be honest, there was also a bit of a personal factor. Seattle felt like a good place to be. There was a lot of industry nearby, a lot of energy around open source, and the group was smaller, so I felt I'd have more freedom to define my own agenda rather than slot into an existing one.

Looking back, I think the lesson I took away is that the best choice was less about ranking programs and more about finding a place where the kind of work I wanted to do was going to be supported, even if it didn't fit neatly into one category. UW gave me that, and I'm very grateful for it.
